opus-5.5.text:
Well, it's the classic chicken-and-egg problem that every new language faces. People use a language because there are libraries, tools, and a community, and there's a community because people use it. Python didn't win because it was the best-designed language for numerical computing. It won because it was there, it was easy, and then NumPy and later PyTorch and TensorFlow got built on top of it. So I'm under no illusion that being better on paper is enough.

That said, I think there are a few things working in TensorLogic's favor. First, it's not asking people to throw away what they know. If you understand tensors and Einstein summation, which pretty much everyone in deep learning does, you're already most of the way there. The key observation is that a logical rule and an Einstein summation are essentially the same operation. A join in a database, a rule in Datalog, and a tensor contraction are all the same thing seen from different angles. So the learning curve is actually quite shallow. You're not learning a new paradigm so much as realizing that two paradigms you thought were different are really one.

Second, it can sit on top of the existing infrastructure. It compiles down to the same tensor operations that run on GPUs today, so you're not giving up the hardware and software stack that the field has spent a decade optimizing. It can interoperate with PyTorch and so on. That lowers the barrier enormously.

Third, and this is the real reason I think it can succeed, there are things you can do in TensorLogic that are genuinely hard to do otherwise. Right now, if you want reasoning, you bolt it on: you prompt an LLM to think step by step and hope for the best, or you glue a symbolic system to a neural network with a lot of duct tape. In TensorLogic, learning and reasoning are the same language. You can write knowledge down as rules, learn the rest from data, and you can even do reasoning in embedding space with a temperature parameter that lets you dial between purely deductive, sound reasoning and the fuzzy, analogical kind that neural networks do. That's something people actually want: models that don't hallucinate, that you can inspect, that you can correct.

The way new languages take over is usually not by converting everybody at once. They find a niche where they're dramatically better, people there adopt them, and then it spreads. So my strategy is to find those applications, where you really need both learning and reasoning, the kinds of places where today's LLMs fall down, and show that TensorLogic does it more simply and more reliably. If that works, the rest tends to follow.

And honestly, AI is a field that's been reinvented several times. The language we use for it today is an accident of history. I think it would be strange if, twenty years from now, we were still writing AI in a language designed in the late eighties for scripting. AI deserves its own language, and I'd like TensorLogic to be it.

r001.rationale: It says that being better on paper is not enough for adoption, but does not state that even universal agreement on TensorLogic’s merits would be insufficient.

r002.rationale: It mentions compatibility with existing tensor infrastructure and PyTorch, but does not identify programmers’ reluctance to rewrite existing Python code as a barrier.

r003.rationale: It does not mention Java, networking tasks, or difficulty doing those tasks in C.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, let me be honest with you: getting a new language adopted is probably the hardest thing you can try to do in computer science. The graveyard is full of languages that were technically superior to what people were using. So I don't go into this naively. But I also think the situation with AI right now is unusual, and that's what gives Tensor Logic a chance.

Here's the thing. Right now, if you look at what people actually program AI in, it's Python plus a library like PyTorch or JAX. And Python is a general-purpose language that was never designed for this. What you're really doing when you write deep learning code is manipulating tensors with Einstein summation, and then wrapping a bunch of Python around it to glue things together. Meanwhile, on the symbolic side, you have logic programming, Prolog, Datalog, and that community has been largely separate. The key observation behind Tensor Logic is that these two things are actually the same thing. A Datalog rule and an Einstein summation are mathematically the same operation. Once you see that, you realize you don't need two paradigms. You need one construct, which I call the tensor equation, and everything else, neural networks, probabilistic reasoning, kernel machines, symbolic inference, all falls out of it.

So the pitch is not "here's a nicer syntax." The pitch is "here's the thing you've been doing all along, made explicit, with the symbolic part thrown in for free." That matters because the biggest problem in AI right now is that we have very powerful but unreliable systems. LLMs hallucinate. They can't reason soundly. And the people who care about that are not going to get there by bolting Prolog onto a transformer. They need something where learning and reasoning live in the same substrate. Tensor Logic gives you that, and it gives you something you can't get in PyTorch, which is a knob between purely deductive, sound reasoning and the kind of soft analogical reasoning that neural nets are good at.

Now, in terms of actual adoption, I think about it in stages. The first stage is researchers, because they are the ones who are frustrated with the current tools and are willing to try something new if it lets them do things they couldn't do before. If you can write a transformer in a dozen lines and then add a logical constraint in one more, that's a concrete win. The second stage is building up the ecosystem: compilers that actually hit the GPU efficiently, libraries, interoperability with the existing Python world, because nobody is going to throw away their code base. You have to meet people where they are. And the third stage, which is the one everyone wants to skip to, is the mainstream, and that only happens if the first two go well.

The other thing I'd say is that I don't think of it as Tensor Logic versus Python. I think of it the way SQL relates to the languages around it. People don't write their whole application in SQL, but when they want to query a database, they use SQL because it's the right abstraction. Tensor Logic can be the right abstraction for the AI part of your system, and the rest can stay in whatever you like.

And finally, I'll admit there's a cultural problem. The deep learning community has been very successful by, frankly, ignoring logic, and there's a certain allergy to anything that smells symbolic. The way you overcome that is not by arguing. It's by showing. You show something that reasons correctly where the LLM fails, you show that it's the same tensor machinery underneath, and you let people draw their own conclusions. That's a long game, but I've been in this field long enough to know that the long game is the only one worth playing.

r002.rationale: It says adoption requires interoperability with the existing Python world because “nobody is going to throw away their code base,” identifying reluctance to rewrite existing code as a barrier.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest challenge is that a language doesn’t get adopted just because it has nice ideas. People have to be able to do something useful with it, and the benefit has to outweigh the cost of learning it and changing what they already do.

So with TensorLogic, the case I would make is that we have these two traditions in AI: learning with neural networks and reasoning with symbolic systems. And we spend an enormous amount of effort trying to connect them. If we can express both in the same language, then that connection becomes much more natural. You can bring knowledge into learning, and you can learn parts of a system that you would otherwise have to write by hand.

But that’s a promise. The way you get adoption is to make it concrete. Here’s a problem, here’s how much work it takes with your existing tools, and here’s how much simpler it becomes with TensorLogic. And it needs to fit into the ecosystem people already use. Asking everybody to throw away their code and start over is a very high barrier.

Ultimately, I think you need a small number of compelling applications. People come because it solves their problem. The fact that it also offers a more unified way of thinking about AI is what can make them stay.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the challenge is that a language has to do more than express good ideas. It has to make somebody’s work easier. If you already have a system that works, why would you switch? There needs to be a concrete benefit: something you can express more simply, something you can learn more effectively, or a result you can understand more clearly.

For TensorLogic, the opportunity is to bring learning and reasoning into the same language. But you have to demonstrate that on real problems. You need examples that people can pick up, modify, and use without having to buy into an entire research programme first.

And you need to meet people where they are. Adoption becomes much harder if the first step is to throw away all your existing tools. So I would think about it as a progression: make it useful for one task, make it easy to integrate, and let people discover the broader possibilities through using it.
